reference_title: EM 1110-1-1905, Geotechnical Design of Shallow Foundations on Soils (USACE, 31 July 2025)

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: [p. 261] Accepting materials or procedures different from those specified or that deviate from the design intent can compromise foundation support and potentially lead to failure or other performance issues. Due to the possibility of unforeseen conditions or non-conformance with established requirements, comprehensive guidance for earthwork observation and testing is difficult to establish. Therefore, the designer should frequently reassess design concepts and assumptions in light of actual conditions observed in the field. This can be accomplished through earthwork observation and testing during construction.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-1, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Quality management
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-2, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Quality assurance
sections.body: [p. 261] Quality assurance. Obtaining quality construction of shallow foundations and associated earthwork is a combined responsibility of the construction contractor and the government. The extent of quality assurance should be commensurate with the value and complexity of the project and the requirements of ER 1180-1-6.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-2a, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria
sections.body: [p. 261] Acceptance criteria. During design, the district geotechnical design element should confirm that the contract specifications include the appropriate earthwork and foundation observation, testing requirements, and associated acceptance criteria. Acceptance criteria may be prescriptive (exact details and instructions are provided) or performance based (desired results are stipulated).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-2b, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Technical responsibilities
sections.body: [p. 261] Technical responsibilities are provided in ER 1110-2-1150 and ER 1180-1-6 for USACE Project Delivery Team members (engineering and construction personnel). Management and administration of the construction contract is the responsibility of the construction team, to include the contracting officer or designated representative.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Geotechnical engineer responsibilities
sections.body: [p. 261] Geotechnical engineer responsibilities. The district geotechnical engineering element should review the project plans and specifications to ensure necessary earthwork and foundation testing requirements are stipulated. These basic services include:
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3a, printed p. 261.

sections.title: Earthwork observation and testing
sections.body: [p. 261] Earthwork observation and testing. During foundation and associated earthwork activities, the geotechnical engineer should remain engaged so that unforeseen conditions or unsatisfactory performance can be effectively managed (via the contracting officer) by the design team according to the design intent. The geotechnical engineer must approve the earthwork and foundation subgrades. For military and civil works projects, the designer of record (DOR) should prepare a short report titled “Engineering Considerations and Information for Field Personnel” or (ECIFP) document as outlined in ER 1110-3-12 and ER 1110-2-1150. This document covers the design intent and critical items to observe during foundation and associated earthwork activities.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3a(1), printed p. 261.

sections.title: Submittal review
sections.body: [p. 262] Submittal review. Designated submittals (such as specialty contractor designs, testing documents) received from the field should be reviewed and approved in a timely manner so that construction progress does not hinder removal, replacement, or modification of unacceptable or unforeseen conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3a(2), printed p. 262.

sections.title: Construction site visits
sections.body: [p. 262] Construction site visits. Construction site visits should be made during critical foundation and associated earthwork activities to observe and compare the field conditions with the design assumptions. For civil works projects, this should be performed according to ER 1110-2-112 and ER 1110-2-1150. Site visits may also be necessary to brief construction division personnel on issues affecting foundation construction that are not suitably conveyed via contract documents or the ECIFP.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3a(3), printed p. 262.

sections.title: Resident and project engineer
sections.body: [p. 262] Resident and project engineer. The designated Resident Engineer (RE) or Project Engineer (PE) are responsible for overall field supervision and quality assurance reporting. The RE/PE or their representative should perform follow-up reviews as needed to confirm/maintain continued acceptability. Field inspections and testing should follow the drawings and specifications and quality management procedures. The RE and PE are assisted by construction inspectors. The Area/Resident Engineer or other responsible individuals in the Area/Resident Office may also be delegated as the Contracting Officer’s Representative (COR) for specific contracts (paragraph 12-4d).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3b, printed p. 262.

sections.title: Construction inspectors
sections.body: [p. 262] Construction inspectors. Construction inspectors are responsible for implementing the field quality assurance procedures. Construction inspectors should understand the critical earthwork and foundation aspects of the project and be familiar with the requirements in the plans and specifications related to foundations and earthwork. Field inspectors should routinely coordinate with the DOR, RE, and PE. Prompt notification should be made of unfavorable or changed conditions that could negatively impact the design.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-3c, printed p. 262.

sections.title: Earthwork observation and testing
sections.body: [p. 262] Once construction begins and progresses, with the support of the construction inspector, the field conditions being encountered should be reviewed for compliance with those assumed for design. This can be done through field and laboratory verification testing and observations.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4, printed p. 262.

sections.title: Foundation subgrade and bearing conditions
sections.body: [p. 262] Foundation subgrade and bearing conditions. Foundation subgrades should be observed, and testing performed to confirm design conditions. Testing should be performed just before foundation placement to avoid degradation of otherwise acceptable soils by construction equipment or environmental factors (such as drainage). Suitable foundation tests may include probing the ground, using a dynamic cone penetrometer (DCP), performing density tests, or other similar methods. Common issues pertaining to shallow foundation support and engineering guidance include:
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a, printed p. 262.

sections.title: Groundwater
sections.body: [p. 262] Groundwater. Groundwater conditions can vary from those indicated in the original field exploration due to natural fluctuations. Saturated or wet conditions exposed at bearing elevations due to groundwater do not necessarily indicate unsatisfactory soils [p. 263] are present. For constructability purposes, groundwater levels are typically lowered at least several feet below bearing elevations. This can typically be accomplished using ditches, sumps, or other dewatering methods. If groundwater seepage begins to exceed the capacity of the dewatering system, conditions should not be expected to improve unless the seepage is caused by recent hydrological events. Where seepage into foundation excavations becomes excessive, excavation operations should be halted until corrective measures are identified and approved by the geotechnical engineer. In some cases, footings can be placed in the wet if the subsurface conditions are acceptable and if the forms permit water to exit during placement (ACI 332).
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a(1), printed pp. 262 to 263.

sections.title: Surface water
sections.body: [p. 263] Surface water. Drainage of surface water into foundation excavations can result in ponded water and consequent delays in construction needed to dewater and de-muck excavation bottoms. Ditches or berms can be used in some cases to reduce water infiltration in foundation excavations due to rain, snow, and other surface water sources. Saturated or high moisture content soils could result in unsatisfactory performance, therefore, wet soils should be removed or modified in a manner to re-establish assumed design conditions.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a(2), printed p. 263.

sections.title: Non-uniform bearing surfaces
sections.body: [p. 263] Non-uniform bearing surfaces. Non-uniform bearing surfaces and isolated areas of harder or firm material (such as cemented deposits, indurated clays, shallow rock) can be as detrimental as soft or loose soil conditions. Zones of harder materials could require removal and replacement with engineered fill to reduce potential differential settlements caused by non-uniform bearing conditions. The extent of removal and replacement, or other ground improvements, must be approved by the geotechnical engineer.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a(3), printed p. 263.

sections.title: Non-level bearing surfaces
sections.body: [p. 263] Non-level bearing surfaces. Bearing surfaces should be relatively flat. Where foundation bases are inclined, the vertical resistance will decrease. Some exceptions include structures where lateral resistance governs (such as T-walls) and the increased lateral resistance is desired and considered during design. In general, bearing surfaces should have a slope no greater than 10H:1V (Horizontal to Vertical). Where necessary, footings can be stepped to change the elevation of the top surface of the footing or where the surface of the ground slopes more than 10H:1V. Stepped and sloping foundations to accommodate unanticipated ground conditions must be approved by the geotechnical and structural engineer.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a(4), printed p. 263.

sections.title: Bearing elevation
sections.body: [p. 263] Bearing elevation. In some cases, foundation bearing elevations can be adjusted in the field to accommodate unsuitable bearing conditions (for example, it may be necessary to lower a foundation to a more competent bearing stratum). The normal method of extending foundations to greater depth is to use unreinforced concrete footing pedestals. Where used, the ratio of the unsupported height to the average least lateral dimension of plain concrete pedestals should not exceed 3. Use of unreinforced concrete pedestals to lower the bearing elevation must be approved by the geotechnical engineer.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4a(5), printed p. 263.

sections.title: Engineered fill supporting foundations
sections.body: [p. 264] Engineered fill supporting foundations. The specified fill and placement requirements should be achieved to perform as designed. Deviations from the earthwork specifications could result in unacceptable performance.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b, printed p. 264.

sections.title: Fill suitability
sections.body: [p. 264] Fill suitability. Prior to placement, proposed fill samples should be tested so that the desired engineering characteristics are established. Typically, soil gradation, plasticity, modified Proctor density and optimum moisture, and soil moisture content should be determined. These parameters aid in soil identification and provide an indication of anticipated moisture conditioning requirements needed during placement and compaction. In some cases, additional testing may be required (such as consolidation, organic content, unit weight) depending on the material source or the foundation soil strength and compressibility characteristics desired. Testing should be performed at suitable intervals to achieve the intended foundation support. Where on-site borrow is used, the testing frequency may need to be increased to account for its natural variability as compared to pit-mined or processed materials that typically exhibit more uniform characteristics.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(1), printed p. 264.

sections.title: Moisture content
sections.body: [p. 264] Moisture content. Proposed fill should be within the specified moisture range prior to compaction activities. Often it is impractical to adjust moisture content in the field by more than about 2 to 3 percent, and particularly where soils contain considerable silt or clay content. Where moisture conditioning (such as wetting, drying) of fill soils is necessary, discing, turning, and sprinkling can be used to achieve more uniform moisture. Indirect methods (such as nuclear gauge) for measuring soil moisture should be verified or adjusted based on direct heat or oven-dry measurements.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(2), printed p. 264.

sections.title: Fill placement
sections.body: [p. 264] Fill placement. Fill supporting foundations should be placed in relatively horizontal lifts that can support compaction equipment. In some instances, the location of fill placement (such as close to adjacent structures) can require reduction of lift thickness or use of alternative compaction equipment to achieve project requirements. After placement and compaction, fill material should be tested for density/relative compaction, and moisture content.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(3), printed p. 264.

sections.title: Proofrolling
sections.body: [p. 264] Proofrolling. Where site space permits, proofrolling may be performed prior to and during fill placement as a visual aid in spotting pumping, soft, loose, or otherwise unsatisfactory conditions. Pumping soils normally contain excess moisture and require scarification, drying, and re-compacting until satisfactory performance is achieved, or the unsuitable soil replaced with suitable compacted material. Proofrolling is particularly useful in structure areas where highly variable fill material is used below foundations.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(3)(a), printed p. 264.

sections.title: Soil compaction
sections.body: [p. 264] Soil compaction. Compaction characteristics of the proposed fill should be established prior to fill placement. Generally, engineered fills are compacted to minimum 95 percent modified Proctor density for foundation support. The modified Proctor energy is comparable to that obtained with the heaviest rollers under favorable conditions (Sowers and Sowers 1979) and has a resulting energy that is about 4.5 times greater than can be achieved using the standard Proctor. The geotechnical engineer should approve modifications to compaction methodologies where the construction contracts use prescriptive specifications.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(3)(b), printed p. 264.

sections.title: Compaction of Free-Draining Soils
sections.body: [p. 265] Compaction of Free-Draining Soils. In some areas, compaction of relatively clean (less than 15 percent passing the No. 200 sieve) and free-draining sands may be necessary for foundation support. The U-shape of the compaction curves for relatively clean sands suggests that the maximum density could occur at either zero percent or 100 percent saturation. Because of the uncertainties associated with laboratory maximum and minimum tests required for determination of relative density, it is often considered desirable to develop compaction control methods based on Proctor values determined from oven-dry samples. For field compaction, clean sands are typically “flooded” (excess water is applied), and only moderate effort using conventional compaction equipment is required to achieve satisfactory compaction.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(3)(c), printed p. 265.

sections.title: Compaction of Variable fill
sections.body: [p. 265] Compaction of Variable fill. In some cases, it can be difficult to adequately identify fill by visual methods alone. In these cases, a “family,” or series of compaction curves can be used for field identification in conjunction with the one-point compaction method. The one-point compaction test can identify the location of the appropriate compaction curve where moisture content of the sample is within a few (1 or 2) percentage points below optimum moisture content. If the point does not fall on a previously identified curve, additional points should be established until the maximum dry density and optimum moisture can be established.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4b(3)(d), printed p. 265.

sections.title: Load and proof testing
sections.body: [p. 265] Load and proof testing. Large-scale load testing is uncommon for verification of shallow foundation performance. Although small-scale load testing (plate load testing) can be performed somewhat efficiently, it is not recommended due to scale effects (limited depth of influence as compared to designed footings) and the potential for long-term consolidation that is not typically evaluated. Where ground improvement methods are used, the installation methods themselves can serve as proof tests. Verification of ground improvement methods is not covered in this manual.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-4c, printed p. 265.

sections.title: Instrumentation and monitoring
sections.body: [p. 265] Shallow foundations and associated earthwork instrumentation may include a combination of devices and methods such as pressure cells, telltales, survey monuments, and settlement plates. Instrumentation monitoring is unique to the needs of a particular project and must be approved by the geotechnical engineer. Application and design of geotechnical instrumentation is not covered in this manual. For additional instrumentation and monitoring guidance, reference EM 1110-2-1908.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-5, printed p. 265.

sections.title: Documentation and communication guidelines
sections.body: [p. 265] Foundation and associated earthwork observation and testing documents should be maintained to provide a record describing field conditions as outlined in ER 1180-1-6. Test locations and elevations should be well documented. These documents are often required to evaluate claims, to implement design modifications (such as future expansion), and to assess foundation performance. Field reports should indicate if the work inspected was or was not completed in conformance to approved construction documents. Project geotechnical and materials completion report requirements are included in ER 1110-1-1901.
sections.applicability: EM 1110-1-1905, Chapter 12 (Earthwork Observation, Testing, and Documentation), paragraph 12-6, printed p. 265.
